newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK activists vow to fight on despite China warning.
newsitem.headline: HK activists vow to fight on despite China warning.

text.p: A warning by China that Hong Kong will no longer be able to mark the anniversary of Beijing's 1989 crackdown on student-led protests stirred cries of foul from the territory's democracy activists on Thursday.
Hong Kong, after more than 150 years of colonial rule, will revert to China next July 1 under a 1984 treaty with Britain called the Joint Declaration.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen's remarks in a newspaper interview on Wednesday were the latest signals from Beijing's communist rulers to unnerve the territory ahead of the handover.
Qian told the Asian Wall Street Journal that Hong Kong would not be able to allow activists to mark the 1989 crackdown or to criticise Chinese leaders.
"In the future, Hong Kong should not hold activities which directly interfere in the affairs of the mainland," Qian said.

He also laid down guidelines for the territory's media after the transfer of sovereignty. "They can put forward criticism, but not rumours or lies. Nor can they put forward personal attacks on the Chinese leaders," he said.

Cheung Man-kwong, a leader of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriot Democratic Movements in China, told Reuters: "Of course, we will continue commemorating those who died in China's democracy movement.
"Commemoration is not illegal under Hong Kong laws," he said.

"China cannot just single out on the law book that the June 4 commemoration is illegal, while allowing patriotic activities to be held in Hong Kong, such as fund-raising galas for victims of flood in southern China," Cheung said.

On June 4, 1989, Beijing sent tanks into Tiananmen Square to put down a student-led protest movement, resulting in heavy loss of life. Hong Kong responded in huge protests that brought up to a million people on to the streets.
The Alliance, which China brands as subversive, commemorates the 1989 deaths with an annual rally and candlelight vigil. Tens of thousands of people turned out for the event this year.
Alliance member Albert Ho said Qian's comment showed Chinese authorities had no respect for the rule of law.
"Every time they give an interview to foreign media, they put new limits on Hong Kong's laws after 1997," Ho said.
"We will fight for the right to continue the commemoration after the handover," he said.

Martin Lee, leader of Hong Kong's biggest political party, the Democratic Party, said in a radio interview Qian's warning showed China planned to force the re-enactment of draconian laws restricting civil rights in Hong Kong.

An editorial in the English-language South China Morning Post urged China-appointed Hong Kong advisers to stand up against any move by China to curb these activities after the handover in 257 days time.
"This blows a hole not only in the Joint Declaration as generally interpreted, but also threatens the powers and position of the future Hong Kong authorities," it said.
"It is a matter which local members of the Preparatory Committee and the chief executive candidates should raise swiftly and firmly," the Post said.
The Beijing-selected Preparatory Committee, which is headed by Qian, is charged with transforming Hong Kong into a Special Administrative Region of China after the handover.
Since 1989, hundreds of Chinese dissidents have fled via Hong Kong to seek asylum in the West. The latest to escape was dissident Wang Xizhe last weekend.
About 80 dissidents live in exile in Hong Kong, and the Alliance is asking foreign countries to take them in before China takes over.
